name: Microsoft
whyItMatters: Largest hyperscaler capex programme in the AI buildout and the primary commercial channel for OpenAI models via Azure. Its data-centre spending sets the demand curve for the entire supply chain below it.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed capex guidance above 80B USD annually, Azure AI revenue run-rate disclosures, and the OpenAI commercial partnership on public record.
risks: AI capex may outrun monetisation for several years
Regulatory scrutiny of the OpenAI relationship
Azure growth deceleration would compress the multiple

name: NVIDIA
whyItMatters: Owns the dominant share of AI training and inference accelerators plus the CUDA software moat. Every hyperscaler capex announcement flows disproportionately to its data-centre segment.
evidenceSummary: Reported data-centre revenue in the tens of billions per quarter with disclosed hyperscaler purchase commitments and multi-year supply agreements.
risks: Customer concentration in a handful of hyperscalers
Custom silicon (TPU, Trainium, MTIA) eroding share over time
Cyclical air pocket if AI capex digests

name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
whyItMatters: Manufactures essentially every leading-edge AI accelerator and controls CoWoS advanced packaging, the single tightest physical bottleneck in the GPU supply chain.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed CoWoS capacity expansion plans, AI revenue contribution guidance, and Arizona fab commitments backed by CHIPS Act funding.
risks: Taiwan geopolitical concentration risk
Capex intensity pressures free cash flow in down cycles
Customer pressure on leading-edge pricing

name: ASML Holding
whyItMatters: Monopoly supplier of EUV lithography, without which no leading-edge AI chip can be printed. Backlog and bookings are a leading indicator for the whole semiconductor capex cycle.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-year EUV and High-NA order backlog with named foundry customers and published bookings figures each quarter.
risks: Export controls limit China sales
Lumpy order timing creates guidance volatility
Foundry capex digestion delays tool shipments

name: Broadcom
whyItMatters: The leading designer of custom AI accelerators (XPUs) for hyperscalers building alternatives to merchant GPUs, plus dominant Ethernet switching silicon for AI clusters.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-billion-dollar AI semiconductor revenue and publicly discussed multi-year custom accelerator engagements with several large customers.
risks: High debt load from serial acquisitions
Custom silicon programmes can be cancelled or insourced
VMware integration execution risk

name: Arista Networks
whyItMatters: Primary supplier of high-speed Ethernet switching for AI back-end networks at Microsoft and Meta. AI cluster networking is shifting from InfiniBand toward Ethernet, which is its home turf.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed AI back-end networking revenue targets and named cloud titan customer concentration in filings.
risks: Two customers drive a large share of revenue
NVIDIA Spectrum-X competes directly for AI Ethernet
White-box switching pressure on margins

name: Vertiv Holdings
whyItMatters: One of the few at-scale suppliers of liquid cooling and power management for AI data centres. Rack densities above 100kW make its thermal portfolio structurally more important each GPU generation.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record order backlog, organic orders growth tied to AI deployments, and a co-development relationship with NVIDIA on reference architectures.
risks: Order timing is lumpy and tied to hyperscaler schedules
Liquid cooling attracts heavy new competition
Margin pressure if data-centre buildouts pause

name: Eaton
whyItMatters: Supplies switchgear, busway, and power distribution across data centres and the grid that feeds them. Electrical equipment lead times stretching to years give it unusual pricing power.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-year electrical backlog and data-centre segment orders growth in quarterly filings.
risks: Industrial cycle exposure beyond data centres
Backlog conversion slower than orders imply
Valuation already reflects electrification narrative

name: GE Vernova
whyItMatters: One of three global gas-turbine manufacturers at a time when data-centre power demand has sold out turbine slots into the late 2020s. Also a major grid equipment and wind player.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed gas turbine slot reservations sold out years forward and published equipment backlog by segment.
risks: Wind segment losses drag on group economics
Turbine capacity expansion could overshoot demand
Execution risk on a young standalone company

name: Constellation Energy
whyItMatters: Largest US nuclear fleet operator and the first to sign a dedicated data-centre nuclear PPA at scale, restarting Three Mile Island Unit 1 for Microsoft. Clean firm power is the scarcest input in the AI buildout.
evidenceSummary: Signed 20-year Microsoft power purchase agreement for the Crane Clean Energy Center restart, on public record with disclosed economics.
risks: Regulatory treatment of co-located data-centre deals
Power price normalisation would compress margins
Nuclear operating incidents carry asymmetric downside

name: Vistra
whyItMatters: Independent power producer with nuclear and gas fleets in the tightest US power markets. Data-centre demand has repriced its entire generation portfolio upward.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed hedged generation margins, nuclear fleet acquisition (Energy Harbor), and ongoing data-centre contracting discussions in earnings materials.
risks: Merchant power price exposure cuts both ways
Heavily owned by momentum funds after a large re-rate
Texas market regulatory intervention risk

name: Modine Manufacturing
whyItMatters: Legacy auto thermal company that pivoted into data-centre cooling, with its Airedale unit supplying chillers and CDUs to hyperscale and colocation customers.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed data-centre segment revenue growth above 50 percent and announced capacity expansions for cooling production.
risks: Legacy vehicular business dilutes the data-centre story
Competes with much larger HVAC incumbents
Customer concentration in a few colocation builders

name: Powell Industries
whyItMatters: Builds custom-engineered switchgear and power control rooms with multi-year lead times. Data-centre and utility orders are layering on top of its oil and gas base, driving record backlog.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record order backlog and growing commercial and data-centre bookings mix in quarterly filings.
risks: Project-based revenue is lumpy
Oil and gas cycle still drives a large share of orders
Capacity constraints limit how fast backlog converts

name: Credo Technology
whyItMatters: Supplies active electrical cables and SerDes connectivity used to wire GPUs inside AI racks. AEC adoption rises with every increase in rack density.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed hyperscaler design wins and revenue inflection driven by AEC shipments to named large customers.
risks: Heavy customer concentration
Connectivity standards can shift between GPU generations
Valuation embeds flawless execution

name: Astera Labs
whyItMatters: Sells PCIe retimers, smart cable modules, and fabric switches that solve signal integrity inside AI servers. Effectively a pure-play toll on GPU rack complexity.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed design wins across major AI server programmes and rapid post-IPO revenue growth in filings.
risks: Competes against in-house silicon at large customers
Post-IPO lockup and insider supply overhang
Single product family drives most revenue

name: Applied Digital
whyItMatters: Converts power-rich North Dakota sites into AI data-centre campuses leased to GPU cloud tenants. A levered, dilution-funded bet on the neocloud buildout.
evidenceSummary: Signed multi-year CoreWeave lease agreements for the Ellendale campus disclosed in filings, with financing packages announced alongside.
risks: Serial equity issuance funds the buildout
Single-tenant concentration risk
Negative free cash flow until campuses fully lease

name: IREN
whyItMatters: Former bitcoin miner redeploying its renewable-powered sites and grid connections into GPU cloud services. Secured power capacity is the scarce asset; the pivot quality is the open question.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed contracted power capacity, deployed GPU counts, and AI cloud revenue figures in operating updates.
risks: Equity raises have funded each expansion phase
Bitcoin mining revenue is volatile and capital hungry
Neocloud pricing could compress as supply arrives

name: Rocket Lab
whyItMatters: The only proven small-launch alternative to SpaceX, with Electron flying at high cadence and Neutron targeting the medium-lift gap. Space systems now drives most revenue, making it a vertically integrated prime in miniature.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed launch backlog, SDA satellite contract awards worth over 500M USD, and published Electron flight cadence.
risks: Neutron development schedule and cost risk
Still free-cash-flow negative
SpaceX price pressure on launch economics

name: Intuitive Machines
whyItMatters: First commercial company to soft-land on the Moon, anchored by NASA CLPS missions and the Near Space Network services contract. A concentrated bet on the cislunar economy actually materialising.
evidenceSummary: NASA CLPS task orders and the Near Space Network contract with a ceiling above 4B USD on public record.
risks: Mission failures directly hit the stock
Revenue concentrated in NASA programmes
Cash burn requires periodic capital raises

name: Redwire
whyItMatters: Space infrastructure roll-up supplying solar arrays, structures, and in-space manufacturing capabilities across civil and defence programmes. Broad exposure without single-mission concentration.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed contracted backlog across NASA and defence programmes plus announced acquisitions expanding the defence drone portfolio.
risks: Roll-up integration and goodwill risk
Thin margins on government cost-plus work
Dilution has funded acquisitions

name: AST SpaceMobile
whyItMatters: Building a space-based cellular broadband network that connects standard smartphones directly to satellites. The addressable market is enormous; the constellation is still mostly unbuilt.
evidenceSummary: Definitive commercial agreements with AT&T and Verizon plus successful BlueBird test satellite calls on public record.
risks: Tens of satellites still needed for continuous service
Repeated capital raises to fund constellation
Launch cadence dependence on third parties

name: Kratos Defense and Security
whyItMatters: Supplies hypersonic test vehicles, jet drones, and satellite ground systems to the Pentagon. Sits across two priority budget lines: affordable attritable aircraft and space resilience.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-year hypersonic flight test contracts and Valkyrie drone programme awards in filings.
risks: Government budget timing slips programmes
Low-margin development contracts
Competition for the collaborative combat aircraft programme

name: HEICO
whyItMatters: Family-run aerospace parts compounder whose electronic technologies group supplies radiation-hardened components into satellites and defence programmes. Quality exposure without constellation risk.
evidenceSummary: Decades of disclosed acquisition-driven revenue growth with defence and space electronics content in filings.
risks: Premium valuation for a parts supplier
Acquisition pipeline must keep replenishing growth
Commercial aero cycle exposure

name: BlackSky Technology
whyItMatters: Operates a high-revisit Earth observation constellation selling imagery and AI-derived analytics to defence and intelligence customers. Real government revenue at micro-cap scale.
evidenceSummary: NRO Electro-Optical Commercial Layer contract award and disclosed multi-year international defence contracts.
risks: Sub-scale against Planet and Maxar
Persistent cash burn
Government contract recompete risk

name: Quanta Services
whyItMatters: The largest specialty contractor building transmission lines, substations, and renewable interconnects in North America. Every AI data centre and grid upgrade ultimately needs its crews.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record total backlog above 30B USD spanning multi-year utility and renewable programmes.
risks: Skilled labour availability caps growth
Fixed-price project execution risk
Valuation re-rated well above historical range

name: Fluence Energy
whyItMatters: Pure-play grid-scale battery storage integrator born from Siemens and AES. Storage is the fastest-growing grid asset class, but integration is a competitive, thin-margin business.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-gigawatt-hour order backlog and deployed storage fleet figures in quarterly filings.
risks: Chinese battery integrators undercut pricing
Project margin volatility
Tariff and domestic content rule changes

name: Cameco
whyItMatters: The western world's largest listed uranium producer with tier-one assets in Saskatchewan and a 49 percent stake in Westinghouse. The default large-cap expression of the nuclear restart thesis.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed long-term contract book with utilities and published production volumes from McArthur River and Cigar Lake.
risks: Uranium spot price volatility
Kazakh joint venture geopolitical exposure
Westinghouse earnings lumpy

name: Oklo
whyItMatters: Sam Altman-backed fast microreactor developer targeting data-centre power with a build-own-operate model. Compelling narrative, but no licensed reactor and no revenue yet.
evidenceSummary: Non-binding letters of intent with data-centre operators and a DOE site use permit at Idaho National Laboratory; first NRC application was denied in 2022 and is being resubmitted.
risks: Pre-revenue with unproven licensing pathway
HALEU fuel supply is itself a bottleneck
Valuation is almost entirely narrative

name: Centrus Energy
whyItMatters: The only US-licensed producer of HALEU, the fuel every advanced reactor design requires. A policy-protected chokepoint as the West rebuilds enrichment independence from Russia.
evidenceSummary: DOE HALEU production contracts and disclosed LEU supply backlog with utility customers on public record.
risks: Revenue still dominated by Russian-sourced LEU resale
DOE funding cadence drives the growth story
Single-site operational concentration

name: Energy Fuels
whyItMatters: Operates White Mesa, the only conventional uranium mill in the US, and is layering rare earth separation onto the same licensed facility. Two strategic-minerals theses in one permitted asset.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed uranium production restarts, commercial NdPr separation runs at White Mesa, and long-term utility supply contracts.
risks: At-the-market equity issuance funds growth
Rare earth economics unproven at scale
Uranium production costs above tier-one peers

name: MP Materials
whyItMatters: Owns Mountain Pass, the only operating rare earth mine in the US, and is building magnet production with the Pentagon and Apple as anchor partners. The centrepiece of western rare earth supply policy.
evidenceSummary: DoD equity investment and price floor agreement plus a disclosed Apple magnet supply deal and operating production volumes.
risks: NdPr price still set by Chinese supply decisions
Magnet manufacturing ramp execution risk
Policy support could shift with administrations

name: Freeport-McMoRan
whyItMatters: One of the world's largest copper producers at a time when grid expansion, data centres, and electrification all pull on the same constrained copper supply. The liquid large-cap copper proxy.
evidenceSummary: Published copper production and reserve figures across Grasberg and the Americas with decades of operating history.
risks: Indonesian policy and smelter obligations
Copper price cyclicality
Declining ore grades raise unit costs

name: NioCorp Developments
whyItMatters: Pre-production developer of the Elk Creek niobium, scandium, and rare earth project in Nebraska. A genuine strategic deposit, but the financing gap is the entire story.
evidenceSummary: Completed feasibility study and an EXIM Bank financing letter of interest, with no construction financing closed yet.
risks: Project financing in the billions remains unsecured
Persistent shareholder dilution to fund overheads
Single-asset development risk

name: Onto Innovation
whyItMatters: Process control and inspection systems with a strong franchise in advanced packaging metrology. HBM stacking and CoWoS expansion directly increase demand for its tools.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record advanced packaging revenue tied to HBM and 2.5D logic inspection in quarterly results.
risks: Semicap cycle downturns hit orders fast
Larger rivals (KLA) push into packaging inspection
Customer concentration among memory makers

name: Camtek
whyItMatters: Israeli inspection and metrology supplier whose tools are used to inspect HBM stacks and advanced packaging interposers. A focused small-cap toll on the same bottleneck TSMC is racing to expand.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record orders for HBM and chiplet inspection systems with revenue growth reported through the AI packaging ramp.
risks: Order momentum tracks the memory capex cycle
Geopolitical risk around Israeli operations
Competition from KLA and Onto in packaging

name: L3Harris Technologies
whyItMatters: Sixth-largest US defence prime with deep electronics, space payload, and solid rocket motor (Aerojet) franchises. A diversified beneficiary of rising western defence budgets.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog above 30B USD across DoD and allied programmes including SDA satellite awards.
risks: Budget continuing resolutions delay awards
Aerojet integration and supply chain issues
Margin targets depend on cost programmes landing

name: AeroVironment
whyItMatters: Maker of Switchblade loitering munitions and small drones proven in Ukraine, now expanded into counter-UAS and space via the BlueHalo acquisition. The clearest listed pure-play on attritable autonomy.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed Switchblade procurement contracts from the US Army and allies plus record funded backlog after the BlueHalo merger.
risks: Programme concentration in loitering munitions
BlueHalo integration risk
Cheaper FPV drones compress the value proposition

name: Ondas Holdings
whyItMatters: Micro-cap holding company selling autonomous drone-in-a-box systems and counter-drone interceptors, mostly to defence and homeland security customers. High narrative torque, fragile financials.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed military orders for Iron Drone interceptors and Optimus systems in the low tens of millions of dollars.
risks: Heavy recurring share issuance
Order book is small relative to valuation
Competes against far better capitalised drone firms

name: Teradyne
whyItMatters: Owns Universal Robots and MiR, the leading collaborative robot franchises, alongside its core semiconductor test business that benefits from AI chip volume. Robotics optionality on a profitable test base.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed robotics segment revenue and UR cobot install base alongside semiconductor test share data in filings.
risks: Cobot demand tied to industrial capex cycles
Robotics segment has underdelivered growth targets
Mobile SOC test customer concentration

name: Hesai Group
whyItMatters: Volume leader in automotive and robotics lidar, shipping hundreds of thousands of units annually into ADAS and robotaxi programmes. Vision sensing is the common input across every autonomy stack.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed lidar shipment volumes above one million units annually and named design wins with robotaxi and ADAS platforms.
risks: US-China tension threatens listing and contracts
Lidar price erosion is structural
Camera-only autonomy approaches reduce TAM

name: Serve Robotics
whyItMatters: Sidewalk delivery robot operator spun out of Uber, with a contract to deploy up to 2,000 robots on Uber Eats. Real deployments, but unit economics remain unproven and funding is equity-led.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed Uber Eats deployment agreement for up to 2,000 robots and published active robot fleet counts.
risks: Heavy ongoing dilution to fund fleet growth
Single-partner revenue concentration
Per-delivery economics not yet demonstrated at scale

name: CrowdStrike
whyItMatters: Leading endpoint and cloud security platform consolidating spend across the security stack. AI both raises attack volume and powers its Charlotte AI detection layer.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed annual recurring revenue above 4B USD with published module adoption and net retention metrics.
risks: Premium valuation leaves no execution slack
2024 global outage created lasting reputational tail risk
Microsoft bundling pressures the mid-market

name: CyberArk Software
whyItMatters: Category leader in privileged access management, now extending identity security to machine identities and AI agents. Agentic AI multiplies the number of credentials that need governing.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed subscription ARR growth and the Venafi machine-identity acquisition broadening the platform.
risks: Integration risk from recent acquisitions
Competition from Microsoft and Okta adjacencies
Subscription transition still maturing into margins

name: IonQ
whyItMatters: The most visible pure-play quantum computing stock, selling trapped-ion systems and cloud access. Genuine research traction, but revenue is tiny relative to a multi-billion valuation.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed contracts with the US Air Force Research Lab and quantum networking acquisitions, with annual revenue still under 100M USD.
risks: Commercial quantum advantage remains years away
Cash burn funded by repeated equity sales
Retail-driven valuation detached from bookings

name: Rigetti Computing
whyItMatters: Superconducting qubit developer with its own fab, selling systems and QPU access to research customers. One of the purest and most speculative quantum hardware exposures on public markets.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed government research contracts and chip milestones, with quarterly revenue in the low single-digit millions.
risks: Repeated dilutive raises keep the company funded
Technology race against far better funded rivals
Revenue does not yet support the market cap

name: Iridium Communications
whyItMatters: Operates a fully deployed 66-satellite L-band constellation serving government, maritime and IoT subscribers under long-term US Space Force contracts. One of the few space operators with a completed constellation and positive free cash flow rather than a promise.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed recurring service revenue, a multi-year EMSS contract with the US Space Force, and published subscriber counts each quarter.
risks: Starlink and direct-to-cell entrants pressure legacy niches
Leverage remaining from the constellation buildout
Growth deceleration in commodity IoT services

name: Globalstar
whyItMatters: Provides the satellite capacity behind Apple's Emergency SOS and satellite messaging features on iPhone, with Apple funding a replacement constellation through prepayments and an equity stake. A rare case of a mega-cap customer directly underwriting a smaller operator's capex.
evidenceSummary: Apple's up to 1.1 billion dollar infrastructure prepayment and 400 million dollar equity investment are disclosed in SEC filings, alongside wholesale service revenue.
risks: Extreme customer concentration in Apple
Apple could shift to alternative providers or in-house capacity
New constellation execution depends on third-party launch and manufacturing

name: Planet Labs
whyItMatters: Operates the largest fleet of Earth-imaging satellites, scanning the planet's landmass daily, and is shifting revenue toward multi-year defence and commercial contracts including NATO work and a large Japanese partner deal. The scale anchor of the listed EO tier.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog growth including a 230 million dollar multi-year agreement with SKY Perfect JSAT and NATO contracts, with quarterly revenue on record.
risks: Imagery prices deflate as the supply of pixels explodes
Government contract concentration
Heavy stock-based compensation dilutes holders

name: ATI Inc
whyItMatters: One of the few Western melters of aerospace-grade titanium and nickel superalloys, the metals that rocket structures, engine components and spacecraft are machined from. Space is a small slice of revenue, but the qualified-mill base beneath the entire theme is this narrow.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-year titanium and superalloy supply agreements with aerospace and defence OEMs; space-specific revenue is not broken out.
risks: Space demand is a small share of a jet-engine-driven order book
Titanium and scrap input costs swing margins
Commercial aerospace cycle downturns hit volumes

name: Voyager Technologies
whyItMatters: Leads the Starlab commercial space station program under a funded NASA agreement, positioning for the ISS retirement transition, alongside a defence and national-security technology segment. A 2025 IPO that turned private space-station ambitions into a listed vehicle.
evidenceSummary: NASA's Starlab Space Act Agreement worth 217.5 million dollars and 2025 IPO proceeds are on public record; commercial station revenue remains prospective.
risks: Starlab needs substantial further capital before operations
ISS transition timing is controlled by NASA, not the company
Post-IPO lockup expiries and follow-on share supply

name: Frequency Electronics
whyItMatters: Builds space-qualified atomic clocks, oscillators and precision timing hardware that guide GPS and secure communications satellites. A genuine micro-cap pick-and-shovel on the satellite subsystems tier with decades of flight heritage.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed funded backlog and contracts supplying timing hardware into US government satellite programs in quarterly filings.
risks: Program timing makes quarterly revenue lumpy
Customer concentration in US government primes
Very thin trading liquidity

name: NextEra Energy
whyItMatters: The largest US utility by market value, pairing regulated Florida utility FPL with the biggest renewables development arm in the country. Its multi-year capital plan is one of the largest single investment programmes in the US grid buildout.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed plans to invest roughly 120 billion dollars over four years plus a multi-gigawatt renewables and storage backlog reported quarterly.
risks: Rate-case outcomes cap regulated returns
Interest rates pressure a capital-heavy model
Renewables policy shifts alter project economics

name: Talen Energy
whyItMatters: Independent power producer whose Susquehanna nuclear plant anchors one of the first hyperscaler power deals, supplying Amazon under a long-dated agreement. It is a template case for merchant nuclear value in a power-short PJM market.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed 2024 sale of its Cumulus data-centre campus to Amazon and an expanded nuclear PPA of up to roughly 1,920 MW running through 2042.
risks: Regulatory scrutiny of large-load deals at nuclear plants
Merchant power price volatility
Concentration in a single flagship asset

name: Hubbell
whyItMatters: Sells the unglamorous essentials of grid hardening - connectors, enclosures, insulators, arresters and Aclara metering - with utility customers generating more than half of revenue. One of the cleanest large-cap expressions of distribution grid modernisation.
evidenceSummary: Utility Solutions segment revenue of roughly 3 billion dollars annually is disclosed in segment reporting, with grid modernisation cited as the growth driver.
risks: Distribution capex pauses when rates rise
Competition from larger electrical peers
Acquisition integration risk

name: Valmont Industries
whyItMatters: A leading maker of steel transmission poles, towers and substation structures alongside its irrigation business. Utility support structures are a direct pick-and-shovel input to every new transmission mile.
evidenceSummary: Infrastructure segment and utility sales are disclosed in quarterly filings, with transmission structures repeatedly named as a growth driver.
risks: Steel cost swings squeeze fixed-price orders
Agriculture segment cyclicality masks grid growth
Utility project timing is lumpy

name: Itron
whyItMatters: The leading US smart-meter and grid-edge intelligence vendor, shifting from hardware cycles toward recurring outcomes software. Its platform sits on tens of millions of endpoints utilities already own.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog of roughly 4 billion dollars and a growing grid-management and outcomes business reported in quarterly filings.
risks: Meter replacement cycles are lumpy
Component supply constraints have bitten before
Utility budgets can favour wires over software

name: Argan
whyItMatters: Parent of Gemma Power Systems, one of the few EPC firms that builds complete gas-fired power plants - exactly the capacity being ordered to serve data-centre load. Backlog has inflected alongside the US gas turbine cycle.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record project backlog approaching 2 billion dollars in quarterly results, dominated by gas-fired power projects.
risks: Fixed-price EPC execution risk
Backlog concentrated in a handful of projects
Valuation now embeds a long gas buildout

name: MYR Group
whyItMatters: Specialty electrical contractor focused on transmission, distribution and substation work plus commercial-industrial electrical including data centres. A smaller, purer T&D peer to Quanta Services.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog of roughly 2.6 billion dollars across T&D and C&I segments in quarterly filings.
risks: Fixed-price project losses have hit margins before
Skilled labour constraints
Customer concentration among large utilities

name: Eos Energy Enterprises
whyItMatters: US maker of zinc-based long-duration batteries positioned as a non-lithium, domestically manufactured alternative for grid storage. A DOE loan and domestic-content tailwinds underpin its Pennsylvania capacity ramp.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed DOE Loan Programs Office guaranteed loan of roughly 300 million dollars plus an orders backlog and opportunity pipeline reported quarterly.
risks: Persistent cash burn and repeated capital raises
Manufacturing ramp and cost-down execution
Competition from falling lithium cell prices

name: American Superconductor
whyItMatters: Supplies voltage-control and power-quality systems (D-VAR) for utilities, renewables interconnection and industrial loads, plus ship protection systems for the US Navy. Grid resiliency hardware is now the bulk of its revenue.
evidenceSummary: Grid segment revenue growth and individual utility and industrial system orders are disclosed in quarterly results and press releases.
risks: Small scale against giant electrical incumbents
Lumpy order timing
History of dilutive capital raises

name: Cleveland-Cliffs
whyItMatters: The only US producer of grain-oriented electrical steel, the core material of transformers, alongside a much larger automotive steel business. GOES scarcity gives a commodity steelmaker a strategic position in the grid cycle.
evidenceSummary: Management has publicly stated that demand for its electrical steel exceeds capacity and has disclosed plans to expand transformer-related production at Weirton.
risks: Automotive steel exposure dominates earnings
High leverage into a cyclical downturn
GOES is a small share of total revenue

name: Southern Copper
whyItMatters: One of the largest and lowest-cost copper producers, with mine lives measured in decades across Peru and Mexico. Grid buildout is a structural demand pillar for the copper it sells.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed annual copper production near one million tonnes and published mine expansion projects in Peru and Mexico.
risks: Copper price cyclicality
Peru and Mexico political and permitting risk
Controlled by Grupo Mexico - governance discount

name: BWX Technologies
whyItMatters: Sole supplier of nuclear reactors and fuel for the US Navy and a leading manufacturer of commercial reactor components and TRISO fuel for advanced designs. It touches nearly every North American nuclear program - restarts, CANDU refurbishments, SMRs and defence - from certified facilities that took decades to license.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record backlog, long-term naval propulsion contracts, and DOE and Canadian commercial nuclear component orders reported in filings.
risks: Government budget cadence drives a large share of revenue
Commercial SMR component demand depends on projects reaching construction
Fixed-price manufacturing contracts carry margin risk

name: Mirion Technologies
whyItMatters: Supplies radiation detection and measurement systems that every reactor, fuel-cycle facility and decommissioning project must install and periodically recertify. An installed-base business earning recurring revenue from the existing fleet, with new builds and restarts adding growth optionality.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed nuclear and safety segment revenue and publicly reported orders tied to reactor new builds, restarts and life extensions.
risks: Carries leverage from its SPAC-era capital structure
New-build order timing is lumpy
Medical segment dilutes the nuclear pure-play story

name: NuScale Power
whyItMatters: Holds the only small modular reactor design certified by the US NRC, with a 77 megawatt uprate approved in 2025, and supplies the RoPower project in Romania alongside majority owner Fluor. Commercial deployment still depends on converting engineering work into firm orders, so revenue remains small relative to the valuation.
evidenceSummary: NRC design certification and the 2025 uprate approval are on record, plus disclosed front-end engineering contracts for the RoPower Doicesti project in Romania; no completed commercial plant to date.
risks: First flagship US project (UAMPS) was cancelled in 2023
Cash burn funded partly through equity issuance
Valuation prices in orders that are not yet firm

name: NexGen Energy
whyItMatters: Controls the Arrow deposit at Rook I in Saskatchewan, the largest development-stage uranium project in the world by planned output. First offtake agreements with US utilities and federal licensing hearings underway make it the bellwether for whether next-cycle supply arrives on schedule.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed feasibility study for Rook I, first uranium sales agreements covering about 5 million pounds with US utilities, and CNSC licensing hearings on public record.
risks: Pre-revenue until Rook I is built and licensed
Large construction capex still to be financed
Single-asset concentration in one mining district

name: enCore Energy
whyItMatters: One of the few new US producers, with in-situ recovery operations at Rosita and Alta Mesa in South Texas actually extracting and selling pounds. Execution has been uneven - guidance resets and a leadership change in 2025 - keeping it in the show-me category despite real production.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed uranium extraction and sales from South Texas ISR operations and contracted deliveries to US utilities reported in filings.
risks: Production ramp has missed prior guidance
Higher-cost ISR ounces are sensitive to uranium prices
Growth funded partly through equity issuance

name: Lightbridge
whyItMatters: Developer of a metallic uranium fuel design aimed at higher power output and improved safety margins for existing and future reactors. Entirely pre-commercial - the story is national-laboratory collaborations and fabrication milestones, not orders or revenue.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed research collaborations with US national laboratories and early fuel fabrication milestones; no commercial contracts or product revenue to date.
risks: Fuel qualification timelines run a decade or more
Funded through recurring equity issuance
Requires HALEU supply that is itself constrained

name: Apple
whyItMatters: The world's largest single buyer of leading-edge silicon and routinely the lead customer on each new TSMC process node. Its in-house A-series and M-series roadmap anchors foundry utilisation and sets the volume baseline the rest of the chain plans around.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed in-house silicon roadmap across all product lines and publicly confirmed purchases of chips manufactured at TSMC's Arizona fabs under its US investment program.
risks: Mature smartphone cycle caps silicon volume growth
China concentration in both assembly and end demand
AI feature monetisation lagging hardware refresh hopes

name: Synopsys
whyItMatters: One half of the EDA duopoly whose software is required to design every advanced chip, now combined with Ansys simulation after a roughly 35 billion dollar acquisition. Every new design start at every node runs through its tools regardless of which chipmaker wins.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-billion-dollar contracted backlog in quarterly filings and the completed Ansys acquisition on public record.
risks: Export-control swings on EDA sales into China
Ansys integration and deal-related leverage
AI-native design tools could reshape EDA economics

name: Arm Holdings
whyItMatters: Licenses the CPU architecture inside virtually every smartphone and a rising share of data-centre and PC silicon, collecting royalties on chips it never manufactures. Armv9 and compute-subsystem licensing lift royalty rates per chip as AI workloads spread to the edge.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed royalty and licensing revenue reported quarterly, with Armv9 adoption and royalty-rate progression discussed on earnings calls.
risks: Valuation embeds aggressive royalty growth
SoftBank ownership concentrates the float and creates overhang
RISC-V adoption as a royalty-free alternative

name: Texas Instruments
whyItMatters: The largest analog chipmaker, building out subsidised 300mm US capacity years ahead of demand to own the cost curve in power and signal-chain chips. Its breadth across industrial and automotive makes it the cycle barometer for the whole analog tier.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-fab US expansion plan exceeding 60 billion dollars and a finalized CHIPS Act award of up to 1.61 billion dollars.
risks: Analog inventory cycle still working through corrections
Heavy capex compresses free cash flow near term
Chinese domestic competition in commodity analog

name: Navitas Semiconductor
whyItMatters: Pure-play gallium-nitride and silicon-carbide power chip designer named by NVIDIA as a collaborator on its 800-volt HVDC data-centre power architecture. It is a small, volatile proxy for the shift from silicon to wide-bandgap power devices in AI racks.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed collaboration with NVIDIA on 800V HVDC data-centre power and design-win announcements, but revenue contribution from data centre is not yet material.
risks: Loss-making with data-centre revenue still ahead of it
Infineon and other large rivals push into GaN and SiC
Cash burn raises ongoing dilution risk

name: Amkor Technology
whyItMatters: The largest US-headquartered OSAT, building a roughly 2 billion dollar advanced packaging and test campus in Arizona next to TSMC's fabs with Apple announced as its first customer. It is the main listed way to own the onshoring of advanced packaging capacity.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed Arizona advanced packaging campus with a finalized CHIPS Act award of up to 407 million dollars and Apple publicly announced as the facility's first and largest customer.
risks: Thin OSAT margins versus foundry in-house packaging
Revenue concentration around smartphone customers
Utilisation swings amplify earnings cyclicality

name: FormFactor
whyItMatters: Leading maker of the probe cards used to test chips at wafer level, where every HBM stack must be tested before packaging. Rising HBM output and known-good-die requirements pull demand for its DRAM probe cards directly.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record DRAM probe-card revenue driven by HBM test demand in quarterly earnings reports.
risks: Memory capex cycles swing orders sharply
Customer concentration among a few DRAM makers
Competition from Technoprobe and Japanese probe-card rivals

name: MKS Instruments
whyItMatters: Supplies the RF power, vacuum, photonics and gas-analysis subsystems inside the etch and deposition tools that Applied Materials and Lam Research ship. Its content per tool rises as chipmaking moves to more etch-intensive 3D structures.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed semiconductor segment revenue and subsystem content on leading wafer-fab equipment platforms in quarterly filings.
risks: Elevated leverage from the Atotech acquisition
Wafer-fab equipment cyclicality hits subsystems hardest
Concentration among a few equipment OEM customers

name: Entegris
whyItMatters: Supplies the filtration, purity control, specialty chemicals and wafer-handling products consumed on every wafer start, with content per wafer rising at each node transition. It is the broadest listed play on semiconductor materials intensity rather than any single chip winner.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed CHIPS Act award of up to 75 million dollars for its Colorado Springs facility and regularly discloses content-per-wafer growth in investor materials.
risks: Leverage remaining from the CMC Materials acquisition
Fab utilisation swings drive consumables demand
Export controls constrain China sales

name: Tesla
whyItMatters: The largest US consumer of battery minerals and a rare case of an OEM integrating upstream, with its own lithium refinery in Corpus Christi and disclosed supply agreements with lithium and graphite producers. Its procurement choices effectively decide which Western mineral projects get bankable demand.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed Corpus Christi lithium refinery buildout plus public supply agreements with producers including Piedmont Lithium and Syrah Resources.
risks: Mineral exposure is a small slice of a story driven by autos, robotaxi and AI narratives
EV demand softness reduces upstream pull-through
Key-person and governance volatility

name: USA Rare Earth
whyItMatters: Building a sintered neodymium magnet plant in Stillwater, Oklahoma while holding the undeveloped Round Top heavy rare earth deposit in Texas. One of the only pure-play US magnet manufacturing stories outside MP Materials.
evidenceSummary: Pilot-scale magnet production and a commissioned innovations lab are disclosed; large commercial offtakes and Round Top development financing are not yet in place.
risks: Pre-revenue with the full commercial magnet ramp still ahead
Valuation ran far ahead of disclosed contracts in the 2025 rare earth rally
Round Top requires separate, unfunded development

name: Novonix
whyItMatters: Developing US synthetic graphite anode production in Chattanooga with a DOE loan commitment behind a planned Tennessee expansion. Graphite is the least Western-secured battery input, and Novonix is one of the few US-listed anode pure plays.
evidenceSummary: A DOE conditional loan commitment of roughly 755 million dollars and disclosed offtake agreements with Panasonic Energy and PowerCo are on record, while commercial-scale revenue remains small.
risks: Chinese graphite pricing undercuts Western anode economics
Large funding gap remains beyond the DOE loan
Customer qualification and production ramp risk

name: Albemarle
whyItMatters: The largest Western lithium producer, spanning Chilean brine, Australian spodumene and global conversion capacity. The default liquid proxy for lithium supply security, though the price downturn forced deep capex cuts and cost programs.
evidenceSummary: Decades of reported production, reserves and conversion capacity with volumes and cost guidance disclosed every quarter.
risks: Lithium price remains below incentive levels for new supply
Chilean royalty and contract renegotiation risk
Capex cuts trade future volume for near-term cash

name: Lithium Americas
whyItMatters: Owns the Thacker Pass project in Nevada, the largest known US lithium resource, under construction with General Motors as joint-venture partner and a closed 2.26 billion dollar DOE loan. The flagship test of whether a US lithium megaproject can actually get built.
evidenceSummary: The closed DOE loan, a 625 million dollar GM joint-venture investment and a GM Phase 1 offtake are all disclosed; there is no production revenue yet.
risks: First production is still years out with ramp risk ahead
Lithium prices sit below feasibility-study assumptions
Phase 2 will require further capital

name: Caterpillar
whyItMatters: The anchor supplier of mining trucks, shovels and power systems that every new Western mine buildout must order years in advance. Resource Industries segment revenue is a direct read on global mining capex, though critical minerals are a minority of it.
evidenceSummary: Reported Resource Industries segment revenue and order backlog disclosed quarterly across decades of operating history.
risks: Mining capex is cyclical and commodity-price driven
Critical minerals are a small slice of total equipment demand
The data centre power narrative already crowds the stock

name: Perpetua Resources
whyItMatters: Developing the Stibnite gold-antimony project in Idaho, the only meaningful US antimony resource, with a final federal Record of Decision received in January 2025. Chinese antimony export controls turned this from a gold story into a strategic minerals one.
evidenceSummary: A federal Record of Decision, Defense Production Act funding awards and an EXIM Bank letter of interest for up to 1.8 billion dollars are disclosed; the full construction financing package is not yet closed.
risks: Multi-year construction with no revenue until first production
Project economics are dominated by gold with antimony as by-product
Financing package not yet complete

name: Ramaco Resources
whyItMatters: A metallurgical coal producer developing the Brook Mine in Wyoming, where drilling indicates rare earth and critical mineral bearing coal seams, with a pilot processing facility groundbreaking in 2025. A rare case of an existing cash-flowing miner funding its own US rare earth entry.
evidenceSummary: An independent techno-economic assessment of the Brook Mine deposit and the 2025 pilot plant groundbreaking are disclosed; there is no rare earth production or offtake yet.
risks: Rare earth grades and recoveries from coal seams are unproven at scale
The core met coal business faces weak pricing
The re-rating already prices in significant rare earth success

name: TMC the metals company
whyItMatters: Holds exploration rights to polymetallic nodules in the Pacific's Clarion-Clipperton Zone containing nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese, and applied for US permits after a 2025 executive order on seabed minerals. The most binary, pre-revenue expression of the theme.
evidenceSummary: The 2025 US executive order on seabed minerals, TMC's NOAA permit applications and a disclosed strategic investment from Korea Zinc are public; there is no commercial production or offtake.
risks: International seabed regulatory conflict is unresolved
No commercial-scale nodule collection or processing has been proven
Environmental opposition and ESG exclusions

name: Palantir Technologies
whyItMatters: Owns the fastest-growing software layer in Western defence, with Maven Smart System and Army NextGen software contracts putting its targeting and C2 stack at the centre of the autonomy shift. It is the reference case for software-defined defence earning technology margins.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed US government revenue approaching a 2B USD annual run rate, an expanded Maven Smart System contract ceiling, and the Army's consolidated NextGen software agreement on public record.
risks: Valuation prices many years of flawless execution
Government procurement politics can shift awards
Stock-based compensation dilutes shareholders steadily

name: Lockheed Martin
whyItMatters: The largest Western prime with the deepest missile franchises - PAC-3, JASSM, LRASM, GMLRS - all running at replenishment rates funded by multi-year procurement. Its order book anchors the munitions tier of the theme.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog around 170B USD and multi-year munitions procurement contracts with the US government and allies in filings.
risks: Recurring charges on fixed-price and classified programs
Heavy dependence on the F-35 program
Continuing resolutions delay award timing

name: Northrop Grumman
whyItMatters: Prime behind the B-21 bomber and one of only two US solid rocket motor producers at scale, a named bottleneck of the entire theme. Its SRM and munitions capacity expansions sit directly on the replenishment critical path.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record backlog above 90B USD and announced solid rocket motor capacity expansions in filings and public releases.
risks: B-21 fixed-price production lots carry loss risk
Energetics and precursor chemical supply constraints
Budget timing slips large programs

name: Elbit Systems
whyItMatters: Israel's largest listed defence firm with combat-proven drones, munitions, electronic warfare and counter-UAS systems, riding European rearmament orders. One of the few public companies spanning nearly every tier of the drone-war stack.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed order backlog above 20B USD with named European munitions and air-defence contract awards in company releases.
risks: Geopolitical and boycott risk around Israeli suppliers
Backlog conversion strains working capital
Export licence dependence for key markets

name: Leonardo DRS
whyItMatters: Supplies force-protection sensors, counter-UAS and short-range air defence content, infrared sensing and electric propulsion for US Navy submarines. A focused defence-electronics house sitting directly beneath the primes on funded Army programs.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed backlog above 8B USD with counter-UAS and short-range air defence program content reported in quarterly filings.
risks: Majority ownership by Leonardo limits float
Program concentration in US Army sensing
Columbia-class propulsion execution risk

name: Mercury Systems
whyItMatters: Makes rugged processing modules and RF subsystems that sit inside radars, EW pods and missiles across dozens of programs. A mid-cap turnaround on the component layer every sensor tier depends on.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record backlog above 1.3B USD and design wins across radar and electronic warfare programs in quarterly filings.
risks: Margin recovery is still mid-turnaround
Program delays create lumpy quarters
Customer concentration among the large primes

name: Howmet Aerospace
whyItMatters: Dominant supplier of investment castings and forged airfoils for jet engines plus fasteners and titanium structures used across defence platforms. Engine-part scarcity gives it unusual pricing power for a parts maker.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record revenue and margins with defence aerospace growth reported in quarterly results.
risks: Commercial aero cycle still drives most revenue
Valuation has re-rated sharply
Titanium input supply and pricing risk

name: Carpenter Technology
whyItMatters: Produces the specialty alloys and titanium products that forgings, fasteners and engine parts start from, with aerospace and defence driving the majority of sales. Sits at the boundary between the raw-materials tier and the forging tier.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed record earnings and a multi-year aerospace and defence backlog, with announced brownfield capacity expansion plans.
risks: Aerospace cycle exposure cuts both ways
Capacity expansion execution risk
Nickel and titanium input cost volatility

name: Red Cat Holdings
whyItMatters: Won the US Army's short-range reconnaissance Tranche 2 program with its Black Widow small drone, converting NDAA-compliance policy into production orders. A genuine small-cap program-of-record story carried by fragile financials.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed US Army SRR Tranche 2 selection and initial production orders in company filings.
risks: Cash burn requires repeated equity raises
Single-program revenue concentration
Production scaling unproven at Army volumes

name: Unusual Machines
whyItMatters: Micro-cap building NDAA-compliant FPV drone motors and components as Western programs are forced off Chinese supply. Disclosed revenue is tiny today; the case rests almost entirely on the reshoring policy tailwind.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed small consumer and component revenue and an announced US drone-motor production facility; defence order book remains limited to date.
risks: Revenue base is very small relative to valuation
Chinese components remain far cheaper without mandates
Equity issuance funds operations

name: Symbotic
whyItMatters: Operates the largest disclosed warehouse-automation backlog in public markets, anchored by a master agreement to automate Walmart's US regional distribution network. It is the clearest evidence that large-scale robotics deployments already have paying customers.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed multi-year backlog above 20 billion dollars anchored by the Walmart master automation agreement, with system deployment counts reported quarterly.
risks: Extreme customer concentration in Walmart
Past accounting restatements on system revenue recognition
Complex share structure limits the tradable float

name: Intuitive Surgical
whyItMatters: The da Vinci installed base of more than 9,000 systems generates recurring instruments-and-accessories revenue on every procedure, the strongest business model in robotics. It defines what mature robot economics look like for every earlier-stage platform in the theme.
evidenceSummary: Reports installed base, procedure growth and recurring revenue mix in detail every quarter.
risks: Premium valuation assumes durable procedure growth
Medtronic and J&J robotic platforms are finally reaching market
Hospital capex cycles delay system placements

name: Procept BioRobotics
whyItMatters: Its Aquabeam robotic system for BPH surgery is winning share with disclosed placement and utilisation growth each quarter. One of the few genuinely mid-cap pure-play surgical robotics names beneath Intuitive.
evidenceSummary: Discloses system placements, procedure volumes and revenue growth quarterly; US reimbursement coverage for Aquablation therapy is on public record.
risks: Still unprofitable and funding growth with equity
Single-procedure concentration in BPH
Competitive response from urology device incumbents

name: Regal Rexnord
whyItMatters: Makes the motors, bearings, gearing and powertrain components that industrial automation already consumes at scale, and management has publicly framed humanoid actuators as a content opportunity. A picks-and-shovels industrial with existing revenue rather than a story stock.
evidenceSummary: Discloses industrial powertrain and automation segment revenue; humanoid-related opportunities discussed on earnings calls without named contracts to date.
risks: Elevated leverage from the Altra acquisition
Short-cycle industrial demand remains soft
Humanoid content is an option, not yet a business

name: Ambarella
whyItMatters: Its CVflow edge AI vision SoCs run perception inference at low power inside robot vacuums, autonomous mobile robots, drones and automotive cameras. A rare mid-cap supplier concentrated in the robot perception-compute socket rather than in robot platforms themselves.
evidenceSummary: Discloses edge AI revenue as the majority of sales and names robotics and automotive design-win categories in earnings materials.
risks: Consumer robotics demand is cyclical
Qualcomm and NVIDIA compete hard at the edge
Customer concentration through ODM channels

name: Amprius Technologies
whyItMatters: Ships silicon-anode cells with industry-leading energy density into drones and light electric aviation, the same spec sheet humanoid and mobile-robot designers need. Energy density per kilogram is a named constraint on robot runtime.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed commercial SiCore cell shipments and revenue growth with named UAS customer categories; robot-specific design wins are not yet on record.
risks: Unprofitable and scaling manufacturing from a small base
Cell giants can replicate silicon-anode chemistry
Customer concentration in defence and UAS

name: Palo Alto Networks
whyItMatters: The largest pure-play security vendor and the loudest advocate of platformisation, consolidating network, cloud and SOC spend onto one stack. Its agreed acquisition of CyberArk extends the platform into identity, the control plane for securing AI agents.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed next-generation security ARR above 5B USD, published remaining performance obligation, and the definitive CyberArk acquisition agreement on public record.
risks: Serial large acquisitions carry integration risk
Platformisation discounts trade near-term revenue for lock-in
Premium valuation leaves little execution slack

name: Fortinet
whyItMatters: The only major security platform that designs its own SPU ASICs, giving it a hardware cost and performance moat in firewalls while it pushes into unified SASE and SecOps. A large installed appliance base entering a refresh cycle underpins near-term demand.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed billings, service revenue and a published ARR breakout for its Unified SASE and Security Operations segments.
risks: Hardware refresh cycles create lumpy growth
Cloud-native SASE rivals attack the installed base
Mid-market exposure is macro sensitive

name: Zscaler
whyItMatters: The reference pure-play in zero-trust network access, inspecting enterprise traffic through its own global cloud rather than on-premise appliances. Its position in the traffic path makes it a natural aggregation point as security shifts to cloud delivery.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed annual recurring revenue around 3B USD with published dollar-based net retention and large-enterprise customer counts.
risks: Firewall incumbents and hyperscalers converge on SASE
Stock-based compensation weighs on GAAP profitability
Growth deceleration would compress a premium multiple

name: Okta
whyItMatters: The largest independent identity provider spanning workforce and customer identity, positioned as the neutral alternative to Microsoft Entra. The rise of AI agents multiplies the machine identities that its platform is being extended to govern.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed subscription revenue above 2.5B USD annually with published remaining performance obligations and customer counts.
risks: Microsoft Entra bundling pressures win rates
Prior support-system breach left a reputational tail
Palo Alto plus CyberArk creates a scaled identity rival

name: SentinelOne
whyItMatters: AI-native endpoint and data-lake challenger to CrowdStrike, with its Purple AI assistant and AI SIEM aimed squarely at automating SOC triage. It is one of the few mid-caps with direct exposure to the AI-SOC shift rather than through a mega-platform.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed annualised recurring revenue around 1B USD with published net retention; profitability on a GAAP basis has not yet been reached.
risks: CrowdStrike and Microsoft dominate the category it attacks
Path to GAAP profitability is still unproven
Platform consolidation squeezes second-place vendors

name: Rubrik
whyItMatters: Turned backup into cyber resilience - immutable copies, ransomware blast-radius analysis and clean recovery - and rode that repositioning through its 2024 IPO. Data security is one of the fastest-growing subsegments as boards treat recovery capability as a disclosure item.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed subscription ARR above 1B USD and growing in fiscal filings following its April 2024 IPO.
risks: Veeam, Commvault and hyperscalers contest the category
Heavy stock-based compensation dilutes holders
Valuation embeds sustained high growth

name: Varonis Systems
whyItMatters: Specialist in data security posture management - mapping who can access sensitive data and detecting abnormal use - which becomes more valuable as enterprises let AI copilots loose on their file stores. A completed SaaS transition gives cleaner unit economics than its licence-era history.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed annual recurring revenue above 600M USD with published SaaS-transition metrics.
risks: Microsoft Purview bundles adjacent capability
Data security is consolidating into platforms
SaaS growth must outrun legacy runoff

name: Leidos Holdings
whyItMatters: One of the largest deliverers of cyber operations and digital modernisation to the DoD, intelligence community and civilian agencies, anchoring the government services tier. Cyber is a segment of a diversified defence-IT business, offering exposure with defence-contractor stability rather than software multiples.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed total backlog above 40B USD with named federal cyber and digital-modernisation contract awards on public record.
risks: Federal budget continuing resolutions delay awards
Recompete losses on large contract vehicles
Cyber is diluted within a diversified revenue base

name: Telos Corporation
whyItMatters: Micro-cap federal security specialist whose Xacta platform automates compliance and risk accreditation for defence and intelligence customers, alongside TSA PreCheck enrollment services. It is one of the few listed micro-caps with genuine security authority inside classified environments.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed federal contract vehicles and TSA PreCheck enrollment expansion, but total revenue remains small and award timing is lumpy.
risks: Heavy concentration in a few government programs
Not yet sustainably profitable
Award and protest timing whipsaws results

name: A10 Networks
whyItMatters: Small-cap provider of DDoS defence and application security appliances sold heavily into service providers, now extending into AI-infrastructure traffic protection. Unusually for its size tier it is GAAP profitable with net cash and returns capital via buybacks and a dividend.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed security-led revenue mix above half of total sales with consistent GAAP profitability reported in filings.
risks: Service-provider capex cycles drive lumpy orders
Scale disadvantage against platform vendors
Appliance-to-software transition risk

name: GlobalFoundries
whyItMatters: Operates the leading DMEA-accredited Trusted Foundry fabs in Vermont and New York, making it the anchor of secure onshore chip supply for US defence and security-critical systems. Trusted fabrication is the deepest upstream link in the cybersecurity trust chain.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed 1.5B USD CHIPS Act award, DMEA Trusted Foundry accreditation, and announced US capacity expansion plans on public record.
risks: Mature-node pricing pressure from Chinese fabs
No leading-edge exposure caps the growth narrative
Fab utilisation swings with auto and industrial cycles

name: International Business Machines
whyItMatters: Runs the most mature superconducting roadmap with a published path toward fault-tolerant systems by decade-end and the largest developer ecosystem via Qiskit. Quantum remains a rounding error inside a 60B-plus USD revenue base, which makes it an anchor on the tier rather than a torque play.
evidenceSummary: IBM has publicly cited roughly 1B USD in cumulative quantum revenue and discloses a Quantum Network of over 250 member organisations.
risks: Quantum success would barely move group earnings
Roadmap slippage on error-corrected milestones
Rivals could leapfrog the superconducting approach

name: D-Wave Quantum
whyItMatters: The only listed pure play selling quantum annealing systems commercially today, including full system sales rather than only cloud access. Annealing is architecturally distinct from gate-model rivals, giving near-term revenue but a contested long-term ceiling.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed the sale of an Advantage annealing system to Germany's Julich Supercomputing Centre, with annual revenue still under 30M USD.
risks: Annealing may be bypassed by gate-model progress
Valuation far ahead of bookings
Equity raises fund ongoing losses

name: Quantum Computing Inc
whyItMatters: Retail favourite pursuing thin-film lithium niobate photonic chips from its Tempe foundry plus photonic computing and sensing products. Market value rests almost entirely on narrative, with revenue among the smallest of any US-listed quantum name.
evidenceSummary: Disclosed small purchase orders including NASA-related contracts and a commissioned lithium niobate foundry, with annual revenue below 1M USD.
risks: Revenue is negligible against the valuation
Repeated dilutive offerings
Unproven positioning across many adjacent markets

name: Coherent Corp
whyItMatters: One of the world's largest photonics manufacturers, supplying lasers, optics and detectors of the kind trapped-ion, neutral-atom and photonic quantum platforms consume. Quantum is a niche slice of a business dominated by AI datacom transceivers, making this a diversified rather than concentrated exposure.
evidenceSummary: Sells laser and photonics product lines used in quantum research but does not disclose quantum-specific revenue.
risks: Quantum demand is immaterial to group results
Cyclical optical communications end markets
Balance sheet still carries acquisition debt

name: SkyWater Technology
whyItMatters: US-based specialty foundry whose advanced technology services include fabricating superconducting chips for quantum developers, with D-Wave a publicly identified customer. Trusted-foundry accreditation positions it for US government quantum and defence programs.
evidenceSummary: D-Wave has publicly identified SkyWater as a superconducting chip fabrication partner; quantum-related revenue is not separately disclosed.
risks: Quantum fabrication volumes are tiny today
Thin margins with customer concentration in development work
Capex needs may require external funding

name: Bruker Corporation
whyItMatters: Its Bruker Energy and Supercon Technologies unit manufactures superconducting wire, and its scientific instruments serve quantum research labs worldwide. Superconducting materials are a small but real slice of an established instruments business.
evidenceSummary: Discloses superconducting wire and quantum-adjacent instrument product lines in its portfolio, without quantum-specific revenue broken out.
risks: Quantum-related sales are immaterial to the group
Soft academic and biopharma instrument demand
Superconducting wire demand is tied to big-science projects

name: Linde plc
whyItMatters: One of the largest global helium suppliers, and the dilution refrigerators cooling superconducting quantum chips cannot run without helium isotopes. Quantum demand is immaterial to Linde today, but it anchors the rawest tier of the chain.
evidenceSummary: Helium is a disclosed part of Linde's industrial gases portfolio; quantum-specific demand is not separately reported.
risks: Quantum is negligible to group earnings
Helium sourcing depends on a handful of global projects
Industrial gas demand follows the macro cycle
